title: French Onion Soup
subtitle: Slow-caramelised onion soup with Gruyère croutons
excerpt: The Parisian brasserie classic: onions caramelised very slowly in butter until sweet and deeply golden, simmered in beef stock and wine, then ladled over bread and covered with melted Gruyère under the grill. Everything depends on patience with the onions.

recipe.sourceNotes: French onion soup (soupe à l'oignon) has roots in French working-class cooking, made with the cheapest and most abundant ingredients: onions and bread. Its association with Les Halles, the central market of Paris that operated until 1969, comes from the tradition of early-morning workers and market porters eating a warming bowl of onion soup after their shift in the cold. The key technique is the long, slow caramelisation of the onions: this is not a dish that can be hurried. The onions must cook for at least 45 minutes, stirring regularly, until they collapse into a heap of sweet, deep-brown, jammy ribbons. A shortcut at this stage produces a pallid, flavourless soup. The wine and cognac (if used) deglaze the pan and add depth; beef stock is traditional and superior to chicken for this application.

content.text: The onions must be caramelised to a deep golden-brown. This takes at least 45 minutes of patient stirring. If the onions start to catch on the bottom of the pan, reduce the heat and add a splash of water. A large quantity of onions (1.5 kg raw) cooks down to a small, concentrated mass; this is correct. Do not use a small pot or the steam will prevent the onions from browning.

items.preparation: thick slices of baguette or sturdy white bread; toasted

content.text: Melt the butter and oil in a large, wide pot over medium-low heat. Add all the sliced onions and a pinch of salt. Cook, stirring regularly, for 45 to 55 minutes until the onions are deep golden-brown and very soft. Do not rush this: the colour is the flavour.

Pour in the wine, increase the heat, and let it bubble for 2 minutes, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom. Add the stock, thyme, and bay leaves. Simmer for 20 minutes. Season with salt and pepper. Remove the bay leaves.

Heat the grill to high. Ladle the soup into 4 ovenproof bowls. Place 2 slices of toasted bread on top of each bowl. Cover generously with grated Gruyère. Place under the grill for 3 to 5 minutes until the cheese is bubbling and golden in patches. Serve immediately.
